name: AT SCHOOL: SEARCHES
safetyNote: Never try to stop a search yourself. Do not grab your bag back, block a door, or run. That turns a school problem into a much bigger one, and it can add a charge that had nothing to do with what they were looking for. Say you do not agree, let it happen, and tell a parent right after.

questions.q: A teacher tells you she is going to look in your backpack. How much reason does she need?

options.text: A good reason to think you broke a rule or the law.
Proof that you broke a rule or the law.
options.explanation: Proof is a much higher bar than school staff need. They can search on a good reason, even if they turn out to be wrong.

options.text: A warrant signed by a judge.
options.explanation: Warrants are for police searches. School staff do not need one to look in a bag at school.

options.text: None at all, because you are at school.
options.explanation: Being at school does not mean anything goes. Staff still need a real reason, and a search has to fit what they are looking for.

questions.hint: The bar is lower than a court needs but higher than nothing. Which one is in between?
questions.principle: At school, the rules for searches are different. Police on the street usually need a strong reason and often a warrant. School staff need less than that. They need a good reason to think you broke a rule or the law. The Supreme Court decided this in 1985 in a case called New Jersey v. T.L.O. A student was caught smoking, and an assistant principal searched her purse. The Court said schools have to keep order, so staff can search with less reason than police. There are still limits. The search has to make sense for what they are looking for.

keyPhrase.quote: At school, they need less reason than police do.
keyPhrase.gloss: Less reason is not no reason. There are still limits.

scenario.setup: Third hour. Your teacher asks you to bring your backpack up to her desk.

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: Someone said you had something you shouldn't. I need to look in your bag.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I don't agree to a search.

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: I still have to look.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. I'm just saying I don't agree to it.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The search still happens. But nobody can say later that you were fine with it.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You have agreed. That takes away anything a lawyer could raise about it later.

scenario.note: Saying you do not agree is not the same as refusing. Do not block, grab, or pull away.

questions.q: A vice principal looking for a stolen laptop has checked your backpack and now wants your wallet. What does the law say?

options.text: A wallet is too small to hold a laptop, so that part goes too far.
A good reason to check the bag lets him look anywhere he wants.
options.explanation: A good reason gets a search started. It does not make the search endless. Staff can only look in places where the missing thing could actually be.

options.text: A wallet is fair game because school owns everything you bring in.
options.explanation: Lockers and school laptops are a different question, and that one turns on your district's own rules. Your own things stay yours, and a search of them still has to fit what staff are looking for.

options.text: A wallet cannot be opened at school without a warrant from a judge.
options.explanation: School staff never needed a warrant here. The limit is not a warrant. The limit is that a search has to match the thing they are trying to find.

questions.hint: The thing they are trying to find decides where they get to search. Could it even be in there?
questions.principle: A school search has to fit the thing staff are trying to find. A good reason gets them started. It does not let them look everywhere. A laptop cannot fit in a wallet, so the wallet is off limits. The case that gave schools the lower bar, New Jersey v. T.L.O. in 1985, set this limit at the same time. Staff can search on less reason than police, and the search still has to match what they are after. A search can start out fine and still go too far.

keyPhrase.quote: That's too small to hold what you're looking for.
keyPhrase.gloss: A search can only go where the missing thing could be.

scenario.setup: The front office. A school laptop went missing during lunch.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Your bag is clear. Open your wallet for me.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: That's too small to hold a laptop. I don't agree to it.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: I would still like to see it.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. Can you write down that you looked in it?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The wallet may get opened anyway. But you said out loud where the line was, and someone at home knows.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The wallet gets opened, and later there is nothing to show that anyone thought it went too far.

scenario.note: Say it, do not do it. Never grab your bag or your wallet back.

questions.q: You tell a staff member you do not agree to a search. She searches your bag anyway. What did saying no actually do?

options.text: It did not stop the search, but it keeps you from being counted as agreeing.
It stops the search, because staff cannot search a student who says no.
options.explanation: Saying no rarely stops a school search. Staff with a good reason can search without your say so. What it changes is what can be said about it afterward.

options.text: It counts against you, because a refusal can be used as proof later.
options.explanation: Saying no is not proof of anything. Staff still have to be able to point to the reason they had before the search started.

options.text: It changed nothing, because letting them do it means you agreed anyway.
options.explanation: Standing there while it happens is not the same as agreeing. You said no once and did not fight, and both of those things are true at the same time.

questions.hint: The search happens. So what is left to gain by saying it?
questions.principle: Saying no does not usually stop a school search. Staff with a good reason are allowed to search without your say so. What saying no does is keep the record straight. If you never say anything, staff can say later that you were fine with it and handed the bag over. If you say no out loud and then let it happen, no one can say that, and a lawyer can still ask whether the search was allowed. Saying no is words, not hands.

keyPhrase.quote: I don't agree to this search.
keyPhrase.gloss: It may not stop the search. It stops anyone saying you agreed.

scenario.setup: The hallway between classes. Staff ask you to hand over your bag.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: I need to go through your bag.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I don't agree to this search.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: I'm doing it either way.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. I'm not going to stop you. I just don't agree to it.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The bag gets searched. But no one can say you were fine with it, and that can matter later.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The bag gets searched, and the only story left is that you handed it over without a word.

scenario.note: Say it once and let it happen. Never hold onto the bag or step in the way.

questions.q: You said they could look in your bag. Now they want your pockets too. What does your yes cover?

options.text: Only the bag. A yes covers what you said yes to, and you can stop it.
Everything from here on, since they have started.
options.explanation: Starting is not the same as opening everything. A yes reaches as far as the words you used.

options.text: All of it now. Stopping halfway looks worse than finishing.
options.explanation: How it looks is not the test. Plenty of people stop for reasons that have nothing to do with guilt.

options.text: Everything, since taking a yes back is not a real thing.
options.explanation: You can stop a search you agreed to. It does not undo what they already saw, and it does end the rest.

questions.hint: Where does their permission come from here?
questions.principle: Most of this chapter is about searches that happen whether you agree or not. This one is the other kind. If staff are going on your yes, then your yes is the whole reason for it, and it reaches only as far as you said. You said the bag, so it is the bag. You can also stop it. Taking it back does not undo what they already saw, and it does end the rest. If they had a good reason the whole time, none of this matters and the search goes on. That is why it costs nothing to say what you agreed to.

keyPhrase.quote: I said the bag. I didn't say my pockets.
keyPhrase.gloss: A yes reaches only as far as you said it.

scenario.setup: The school office. Your bag is already open on the counter.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Pockets too. Empty them out.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I said you could look in the bag.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Same thing.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: It isn't. I only said the bag.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The pockets are a separate question now, and somebody has to answer it.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: One yes at the start covers everything that happens after it.

scenario.note: If they never had a reason, your yes is the whole search. Say what it covered.

questions.q: A friend tells you to delete your photos before staff look at your phone. What actually happens if you do?

options.text: Deleting does not clear it, and it can turn a small problem into a bigger one.
Deleting clears it, because a deleted photo is gone.
options.explanation: A photo can still sit in a backup, on someone else's phone, or in a group chat. Deleting your copy does not reach any of those.

options.text: Deleting is safe, because whatever staff find at school stays at school.
options.explanation: What staff find can go to police, and a school report can start a case. It does not stop at the office door.

options.text: Deleting looks better than refusing, since refusing makes you seem guilty.
options.explanation: Saying no is not proof of anything. Getting rid of something after you were asked for it is the part that can look bad.

questions.hint: Ask where else the same picture already sits.
questions.principle: Deleting is not the safe move it feels like. A photo you delete can still sit in a cloud backup, on someone else's phone, or in a group chat you do not control. Police can also ask a company for it later. And getting rid of something after you have been asked for it can become its own problem, on top of whatever they were looking at. If you think something on your phone matters, the person to talk to is a parent or a lawyer, not the group chat.

keyPhrase.quote: Deleting it does not make it gone.
keyPhrase.gloss: You can delete your copy. You cannot delete theirs.

scenario.setup: The cafeteria. Word is going around that staff are checking phones.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: Delete everything before they get to you.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: That doesn't make it gone.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: Nobody checks the cloud.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'm not deleting anything. I'll talk to my mom tonight.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Whatever happens next is about the photo. Nothing new got added on top of it.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The copies are still out there, and now there is a second thing to explain.

scenario.note: Do not delete, and do not hand your phone around to friends either.

questions.q: The search is over and you think it was not fair. What is the most useful thing to do that night?

options.text: Write down what happened while it is fresh, and tell a parent.
Nothing, because an unfair search cancels the punishment anyway.
options.explanation: School discipline does not fall apart on its own when a search was improper. Somebody has to raise it for you.

options.text: Go back tomorrow and argue it with the staff member who did it.
options.explanation: Arguing with the person who did it rarely changes it, and it can add a second problem to the first one.

options.text: Clear anything off your phone that could come up later.
options.explanation: Copies usually sit somewhere you do not control, and clearing things out after the fact can become its own problem.

questions.hint: Ask which of these still helps you in a week.
questions.principle: The time to sort out an unfair search is after it, not during it. Write down what happened while you still have it clear: who, when, what was said, who else saw it. Tell a parent that night. If the school takes action, ask for the reason in writing. A search that was not proper does not undo school discipline on its own, so someone may have to raise it for you. That is what a parent, an advocate, or a lawyer is for. None of this works as well a week later, when everyone tells it differently.

keyPhrase.quote: Write it down tonight, while you still have it clear.
keyPhrase.gloss: Details fade fast, and later on you will need them.

scenario.setup: Your kitchen table that night. Your bag is still by the door.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: So what actually happened?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: They went through my bag in front of everybody.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Did they say why?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: No. I'm writing down what I have before I lose it.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You have names, times, and words while they are still right.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: In a week it is your word against a report that was written the same day.

scenario.note: Write it for yourself first. Deciding what to do with it can wait until morning.

questions.q: A staff member says she will call police unless you open your bag yourself. What does opening it get you?

options.text: It gets you nothing you can count on. The call can happen anyway, and now you agreed.
It keeps police out of it, since staff deal with what they find themselves.
options.explanation: Staff can call police whether you open it or not. Handing over the bag does not buy that decision.

options.text: It shows you are cooperating, which usually earns you a break.
options.explanation: The person searching you does not decide what happens next. Cooperating is not a deal, because nobody on that side is offering one.

options.text: It changes nothing, since opening it yourself is not the same as agreeing.
options.explanation: Opening it yourself is the clearest way to agree there is. After that, nobody has to show they had a reason at all.

questions.hint: Who gets to decide if police are called?
questions.principle: A trade like this is not really a trade. Whether police get called is usually not up to the person in front of you, and it can happen either way. What opening the bag does do is settle the consent question. Once you open it yourself, nobody has to show they had a good reason. You can say no and still be polite, and you can let a search happen without helping it along. Those are two different things, and the difference is the whole point.

keyPhrase.quote: I'm not opening it. I'm not going to stop you either.
keyPhrase.gloss: Not helping is not the same as fighting.

scenario.setup: The principal's office. Your bag is on the chair next to you.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Open it, or I call the police.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'm not opening it.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: That choice is going to look bad.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I understand. I'm not going to stop you from looking.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The bag may get opened anyway, and the call may happen anyway. Neither one is on you.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You opened it, so the reason never has to be explained, and the call can still happen.

scenario.note: Say no with words. Do not hold the bag, and do not walk out of the room.

questions.q: A staff member says she is not searching you, she is just taking a look. Does the name change anything?

options.text: No. Going through your things is a search whatever anyone calls it.
Yes. A look is casual, so the rules about searches do not apply.
options.explanation: The rules follow what is happening, not the word for it. Casual is a tone, not a legal test.

options.text: Yes. It only counts as a search when an officer is the one looking.
options.explanation: School staff searching you is a school search. It has its own rules and it counts.

options.text: No. And because it is a search, she needs a warrant before she can look.
options.explanation: Warrants are for police. School staff need a good reason, and that is a lower bar than a warrant.

questions.hint: The word she uses does not change what her hands are doing.
questions.principle: What something is called does not change what it is. If a staff member goes through your bag, your pockets, or your phone, that is a search, and it needs the same good reason any school search needs. Calling it a look, a check, or a quick peek does not lower the bar. It matters later, because if it was a search, then whether there was a reason for it is a fair thing to ask. It matters now too, because you can say you do not agree to a look just as easily as to a search.

keyPhrase.quote: Call it what you want. I don't agree to it.
keyPhrase.gloss: A search by another name follows the same rules.

scenario.setup: The hallway. She is already unzipping the front pocket.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Relax. This isn't a search, I'm just taking a look.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I don't agree to it, whatever it's called.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It isn't that serious.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. I'm still not agreeing to it.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: It is on the record as a search, which is what it was.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It goes down as a look you were fine with, and the reason never gets asked about.

scenario.note: You can be calm and still disagree. Tone is not the same as agreeing.

questions.q: An officer at school asks a staff member to search your bag for him. Why does that matter?

options.text: It can raise the bar to the one police work from, instead of the school one.
It makes no difference, because he is at school and not out on the street.
options.explanation: The same officer has the same job in both places. Being inside a school does not make it a smaller thing.

options.text: It means a warrant is needed now, because police are the ones asking.
options.explanation: It does not go straight to a warrant. What can change is the level of reason needed, not the paperwork.

options.text: It means whatever turns up can only be used by police, not by the school.
options.explanation: Both can act on it. School discipline and a case run on their own rules and neither waits for the other.

questions.hint: Ask whose search it really is when someone else asked for it.
questions.principle: Who is really running a search matters. School staff work from a lower bar than police do. When an officer asks staff to search for him, courts have said that can change which rules apply, because the school is doing police work. It is not automatic, and it is not settled the same way everywhere. What you do is the same either way. Say you do not agree, do not physically stop it, and tell a parent right after. Whether the bar shifted is a question for a lawyer, later.

keyPhrase.quote: I don't agree to this search, and I want my mom called.
keyPhrase.gloss: Say it the same way, whoever is doing the asking.

scenario.setup: A small room off the school office. An officer waits by the door.

lines.label: SRO
lines.text: Go ahead and check the bag for me.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Empty it out on the table.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can someone call my mom before this starts?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: We'll get to that.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. I'm not going to stop you.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Who asked for the search is now part of the story, and a lawyer can use that.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It reads as a school search you were fine with, and the officer never appears in it.

scenario.note: Ask who is asking, then say the same words. Do not argue about which rules apply.

questions.q: Money goes missing at practice and the coach tells the whole team to empty their bags. What is different about a search like that?

options.text: It is aimed at everyone at once, which is the weakest kind of reason.
It is stronger, because covering everyone means nobody got singled out.
options.explanation: Searching everybody is not fairer, it is thinner. A school search normally has to point at a person.

options.text: It is fine, because somebody on the team obviously took it.
options.explanation: That somebody did it is not a reason to think you did. A reason has to be about you.

options.text: It works out fine once the money turns up in somebody's bag.
options.explanation: Whether a search was allowed is decided by what staff knew before it started, not by what it turned up.

questions.hint: Ask who it is actually pointed at.
questions.principle: A school search normally has to point at a person. Staff need a good reason to think you broke a rule, not that the room did. A search of everyone at once is the weakest version of that, and courts look at it hardest. It is not the same as a metal detector at the door. That one is quick, treats everyone alike, and is not about catching one person. If a whole group gets searched over one missing thing, saying you do not agree is worth more than usual. There may have been no reason aimed at you at all.

keyPhrase.quote: I don't agree. Nobody said anything about me.
keyPhrase.gloss: A reason aimed at the room is not a reason aimed at you.

scenario.setup: The locker room after practice. Bags in a line on the bench.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Everybody. Bags out on the bench.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Did somebody say it was me?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: I'm not doing this one at a time.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Then I'd like that written down somewhere.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Your bag gets looked through with everyone else's, and the missing reason is on the record.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It looks like the whole team agreed, so nobody has to explain why anyone was searched.

scenario.note: Do not make it a standoff in front of the team. Say it once and let it go.

questions.q: A staff member tells you to open your backpack and take everything out yourself. What is the best move?

options.text: Do what she says with your hands, and say out loud that you do not agree.
Do it, since doing it yourself keeps it from counting as a search.
options.explanation: It counts either way, and doing it yourself can be treated as agreeing to it.

options.text: Refuse to touch it, since making them do it stops the search.
options.explanation: It rarely stops anything. It usually adds a discipline problem on top of the search.

options.text: Do it fast and say nothing, since arguing only makes it worse.
options.explanation: Saying you do not agree is not arguing. Saying nothing is the part that reads as agreeing.

questions.hint: Your hands and your words can do two different things.
questions.principle: Doing it yourself is still a search, and it can be treated as agreeing to one. That is the part most people have backwards. It is also true that refusing to move rarely stops anything and can turn a search into a discipline problem. So split it. Let your hands cooperate and let your words object. Open the bag if you are told to, and say clearly that you do not agree to the search. You have then done everything you can safely do, and you have not handed anyone your consent.

keyPhrase.quote: I'll do what you're telling me. I don't agree to it.
keyPhrase.gloss: Hands cooperate. Words object. Both at the same time.

scenario.setup: A classroom after the bell. She is waiting by the door with your bag.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Take everything out, please.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'll do it. I don't agree to the search.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Noted.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The bag gets emptied and the objection stands. You gave up nothing you did not have to.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It looks like you offered, and later there is no difference between told and offered.

scenario.note: This is the move for almost every school search: do the thing, say the words.

questions.q: Staff find something in your bag and ask you to explain it. What happens if you do?

options.text: What you say can travel to a case, even though a teacher is the one asking.
Not much, since being honest early clears things up.
options.explanation: Sometimes it does. Sometimes it fills in the part nobody could prove, and you cannot tell which from inside the room.

options.text: It helps you, since you did nothing wrong and it will show.
options.explanation: Being innocent does not make explaining safe. People who did nothing wrong still say things that get used.

options.text: It stays at school, since a teacher is not the police.
options.explanation: A staff member can be asked later what you told them, and a school report can be part of a case.

questions.hint: Ask who else could end up reading it.
questions.principle: A teacher asking you to explain is not a police interview, and it can still reach one. Staff can be asked later what you told them, and school reports can become part of a case. That does not make the teacher your enemy. It makes the moment worth slowing down. You can be polite, say you would rather not explain right now, and ask to call a parent. If it turns out to be nothing, you lost nothing. If it turns out to be something, you did not hand over the one thing nobody else could give them.

keyPhrase.quote: I'd rather not explain it until my mom is here.
keyPhrase.gloss: Polite and quiet are not opposites.

scenario.setup: A back room off the gym. What they found is on the table.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: So what is this?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'd rather not explain it until my mom is here.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It's easier if you just tell me now.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I understand. I'd still like to wait for her.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The thing is still there, and your account of it is not.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Your explanation exists now, and it can be repeated by someone else later.

scenario.note: You can answer where the bathroom is and still not answer this.

questions.q: Staff want to look in your hall locker. How is that different from your backpack?

options.text: It is the school's locker, and Michigan law says to expect no privacy in it.
It is no different, since a locker needs a warrant like anything else.
options.explanation: No warrant is needed for a locker. Michigan has a law that says so, and every district writes a policy under it.

options.text: It is yours as soon as you put your own lock on it.
options.explanation: A lock you bought does not change who owns the locker. The school still does, and the rule follows the owner.

options.text: It is the school's, so everything in your backpack is theirs too.
options.explanation: The locker rule stops at the locker. A bag you carry is yours, and searching it takes the usual good reason.

questions.hint: Whose locker is it, before anything goes in it?
questions.principle: A locker is not a backpack. Michigan has a law about this. A student who uses a school locker is treated as having no privacy in it or in what is inside. Every district has to write a locker policy and hand it to students, and a principal can search a locker under that policy. Police can help if the principal asks. Your own lock does not change any of it. What is in your bag or your pockets is a different question with the usual rules, so it is worth knowing which one you are standing in front of.

keyPhrase.quote: The locker is the school's. My bag is not.
keyPhrase.gloss: Different things you keep, different rules.

scenario.setup: The hallway between classes. Two staff are standing at your locker.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: We are going to open this.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Is my backpack part of that?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Should it be?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: It is not in the locker. I don't agree to that part.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The locker gets opened, which was always going to happen, and the bag is a separate question.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The locker and the bag become one search, and the easy rule ends up covering both.

scenario.note: The locker is not the thing to argue about. What you carry is the part with a rule behind it.

questions.q: A dog goes down the hallway and stops at your bag. What does that let staff do?

options.text: Open that bag. It does not open your pockets, your phone, and your car.
Open anything of yours, since the dog picked you out of the line.
options.explanation: A reaction points at one thing. It does not turn into permission for everything you own.

options.text: Nothing at all, since a dog cannot give anybody a reason.
options.explanation: A reaction is one of the ways staff get a reason. It is the step before a search, not nothing.

options.text: Search everyone standing there, since the dog worked the whole line.
options.explanation: A reason has to be about a person. Being in the same hallway is not one.

questions.hint: The dog pointed at one thing. What was it?
questions.principle: A dog walking past bags in a hallway is usually not treated as a search of you. Nothing of yours gets opened. What a reaction does is give staff a reason, and a reason is always about one thing. If the dog reacts to your bag, that is a reason to open your bag. It is not a reason to go through your pockets, your phone, or the bag next to yours. Courts do not agree on every part of this. So keep it simple. Stand still, ask what they are opening, and say you do not agree.

keyPhrase.quote: The dog stopped at my bag, not at me.
keyPhrase.gloss: A reason points at one thing at a time.

scenario.setup: The main hallway. A handler and a dog are working down the line of students.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Everyone step back from the bags.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: This one. I'm going to open it.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Just that one? I don't agree to it either way.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: One bag gets opened, and the line between that bag and everything else got said out loud.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: One reaction turns into a search of whatever anyone feels like opening.

scenario.note: Never move toward a working dog or reach for your bag. Stand still and use words.

questions.q: You joined the track team and the school says you can be drug tested at random. How does that work?

options.text: Testing for a team is one of the few checks that needs no reason.
They still need a reason to think you used something.
options.explanation: Team testing is an exception. Courts have allowed it without any suspicion, because playing is a choice.

options.text: Signing up means staff can go through your things too.
options.explanation: The exception is narrow. Being on a team does not open your bag, your phone, or your car.

options.text: Being a student is enough, so the school can test anyone.
options.explanation: It is not enough. The cases that allow this are about students who chose an activity, not every student.

questions.hint: Ask what you signed up for, and what the test is for.
questions.principle: Most school searches need a reason aimed at a person. Team drug testing is one of the exceptions. Courts have allowed schools to test students who choose to play sports, with no suspicion at all, because joining is a choice and the testing is narrow. The Supreme Court said so in 1995 and again in 2002. Narrow is the key word. It is a test for drugs, and it is not a reason to go through the rest of your things. The details of how a district runs it are in the athletic policy, which is worth reading before the season.

keyPhrase.quote: Testing for the team is not a search of everything else.
keyPhrase.gloss: One exception does not open the rest.

scenario.setup: The gym before practice. A sheet with names on it goes around.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Anyone on this list, see me after warmups.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Is this the random one?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It is.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. Does it cover anything besides that?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know what it covers, which is the part most people never ask about.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You find out what it covered afterward, when there is nothing to do about it.

scenario.note: This is a question to ask before the season, not during it. Ask for the policy in writing.

questions.q: Staff search your car over a vape and find something else in the glove box. What decides whether they can use it?

options.text: Whether the glove box was somewhere a vape could be.
Nothing. They were only allowed to look for a vape.
options.explanation: If they were allowed to look there, what is sitting there counts. The limit is the place, not the label on it.

options.text: The fact they found it, which now lets them look anywhere.
options.explanation: Finding one thing does not widen the search. Each new place still has to fit a reason.

options.text: Whether the car counts as school property, and it does not.
options.explanation: The lot is school property. Parking there does not put your car out of reach.

questions.hint: Were they allowed to be looking there?
questions.principle: If staff are allowed to look somewhere, what they find there counts. A search for a vape lets them open the glove box, so whatever is in the glove box is in front of them. That is the same rule running forward, not a loophole. The limit is still the place. If a vape could not fit somewhere, they should not have been looking there, and what turns up there is a different argument. The lot is school property, which is what lets the school bar apply at all.

keyPhrase.quote: Was that somewhere they were allowed to look?
keyPhrase.gloss: What counts depends on where they were allowed to be.

scenario.setup: The student lot after sixth hour. The passenger door is open.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: What is this?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'm not going to explain it.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It was sitting right there.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I understand. I'd like to call my mom.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The thing is on the table and your account of it is not.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You explain it once here, and then again to whoever gets called.

scenario.note: Where they were allowed to look is an argument for later. Do not have it in the parking lot.

questions.q: Staff are looking for a missing calculator. They find it in your bag, then keep going through the rest. What is true now?

options.text: The reason ended when they found it, so the rest is a new search.
The reason holds until they finish the whole bag.
options.explanation: A search runs on its reason. When the thing turns up, there is nothing left to look for.

options.text: The reason grows, since finding one thing shows they were right.
options.explanation: How it turned out does not change what they were allowed to do. That was set before they started.

options.text: The reason never mattered, since school bags can be checked anytime.
options.explanation: Bags are not open season at school. Staff need a reason to start and the reason has a size.

questions.hint: What were they looking for, and do they still need to look?
questions.principle: A search runs on its reason. When the reason is gone, the search should be too. If staff are looking for a calculator and the calculator turns up, there is nothing left to look for. Going through the rest of the bag after that is a new search, and it needs a reason of its own. This is one of the easiest limits to notice while it is happening, and one of the easiest to lose by saying nothing. Naming it out loud is what puts it on the record.

keyPhrase.quote: You found it. What are you looking for now?
keyPhrase.gloss: When the reason ends, the search should end.

scenario.setup: A classroom after the bell. The calculator is already on the desk.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Good, here it is.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: So we're done?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Let me just check the rest.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can you write down that you found it?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The second search is a second search, and everyone in the room heard that.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It all reads as one search that nobody had a reason to stop.

scenario.note: Ask the question first. It is easier to say than a speech about limits.

questions.q: A staff member asks you to pull up the group chat and show her yourself. What happens if you do?

options.text: You agreed to that much, and it gets easier for anyone to go further.
Nothing counts, since you were the one holding the phone.
options.explanation: Doing it yourself is the clearest way to agree. It is the version nobody has to explain later.

options.text: It is not really a search, since she only read it over your shoulder.
options.explanation: Reading your messages is a search of your messages. Where she was standing does not change that.

options.text: It clears things up, since she sees the whole thing right away.
options.explanation: Sometimes it does. Sometimes it fills in the part nobody had, and you cannot tell which from inside the room.

questions.hint: Whose hands are on it does not decide much.
questions.principle: Showing something yourself is the clearest way to agree to it. If a staff member asks and you scroll to it, nobody later has to explain what reason there was, because you handed it over. It also tends to widen. One message becomes the thread, and the thread becomes the phone. You can hand a phone over when you are told to and still say you are not going to open anything on it. Doing what you are told and agreeing to a search are two different things, and this is the moment that shows the difference.

keyPhrase.quote: You can hold the phone. I'm not opening it.
keyPhrase.gloss: Showing it yourself is agreeing to it.

scenario.setup: The cafeteria at lunch. She is standing at the end of your table.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Just pull up the chat and show me.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'd rather not open it.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It will take two seconds.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: You can hold the phone. I'm not opening it.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Whatever happens next, it did not happen because you opened it.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: One message is open, and the rest of the phone is right there next to it.

scenario.note: Hand the phone over if you are told to. Opening it is the part that is yours to decline.

questions.q: After the search, staff write it up and ask you to say you agreed to it. What should you do?

options.text: Say what actually happened: you did not agree, and you did not fight.
Say you agreed, because a written refusal can come back on you.
options.explanation: A refusal is not proof of anything, on paper or out loud. What gets written down is what survives.

options.text: Stay quiet and let the paperwork say what it says.
options.explanation: Staying quiet does not leave it open. It leaves their version as the only one.

options.text: Agree with it, since you did open the bag when you were told to.
options.explanation: Doing what you were told is not the same as agreeing. Both of those can be written down.

questions.hint: The paper is going to outlive the memory.
questions.principle: What gets written down is what people have later. If staff write that you agreed, that is the version that survives, and nobody has to explain what reason they had. You do not have to sign anything or say anything. You can say plainly what happened instead: you did not agree, and you did not resist. Both of those are true at once. If you are not sure what a paper says, you can say you would rather a parent read it first.

keyPhrase.quote: I didn't agree, and I didn't stop you.
keyPhrase.gloss: Both halves are true. Say both.

scenario.setup: A quiet corner of the cafeteria. A form is turned around toward you.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Sign here that you were okay with it.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I didn't agree to it. I also didn't stop you.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It's just paperwork.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'd rather my mom read it first.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The paper says what happened, which is the only thing anyone will have in a month.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The paper says you agreed, and there is nothing next to it saying otherwise.

scenario.note: You can decline to sign without arguing. Say it once and ask for a parent.

questions.q: The school officer asks you questions while staff go through your bag. What is true about his questions?

options.text: You can say you are not answering, whoever is doing the asking.
You have to answer him, since he works at the school every day.
options.explanation: Where he works does not change what you can do. You can decline to answer anyone at school.

options.text: They do not count, because nobody read you any rights.
options.explanation: A warning is only required in certain situations, and what you say can matter with or without one.

options.text: They help you, since explaining now keeps it out of court.
options.explanation: Explaining now is how things get into court. Nobody in the room decides what happens next.

questions.hint: The uniform did not change jobs when it walked inside.
questions.principle: You can decline to answer questions at school, whether it is a teacher, an administrator, or the officer who works in the building. That part is not complicated. What is less settled is which rules apply to an officer inside a school, and courts have gone different ways on it. You do not have to sort that out while it is happening. Let staff look if they are going to look, say you are not answering questions, and ask for a parent. The rest is a lawyer's problem later.

keyPhrase.quote: I'm not answering questions. Please call my mom.
keyPhrase.gloss: A school officer is still an officer.

scenario.setup: The locker room, second period. Your bag is open on the bench.

lines.label: SRO
lines.text: Just tell me what I'm going to find.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'm not answering questions.

lines.label: SRO
lines.text: It is easier if you say it now.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'm not answering questions. Can someone call my mom?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The bag is searched and nothing you said is part of it.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The search finds what it finds, and your words are attached to all of it.

scenario.note: The search and the questions are two different things. You can allow one and refuse the other.

questions.q: Your mom is on the phone and tells staff they can go ahead and search your bag. What does that change?

options.text: Not much. Staff did not need her word, and you can still say you do not agree.
Everything, since a parent can agree to it for you.
options.explanation: At school staff did not need her permission in the first place, so giving it does not unlock anything.

options.text: Staying quiet now is the same as going along with it.
options.explanation: Your part is still yours. You can say you do not agree whatever anyone else said.

options.text: It keeps the whole thing inside the school building.
options.explanation: What staff find can go to police either way. A parent agreeing does not keep it inside the building.

questions.hint: Whose agreement were they missing in the first place?
questions.principle: At school, staff do not need a parent's permission to search, so a parent saying yes does not unlock anything that was locked. It also does not take away what you can say. You can still say you do not agree, and it still means what it meant before. What the phone call is good for is different. Somebody now knows what is happening, and somebody can ask questions afterward that a student cannot ask. Ask for the call even when you expect the answer to be yes.

keyPhrase.quote: I still don't agree, and I'm glad she knows.
keyPhrase.gloss: A parent's yes does not replace your no.

scenario.setup: The coach's room by the gym. The phone is on speaker.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Your mom says go ahead.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Just let them look, it's fine.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. I'm not stopping them. I still don't agree to it.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Noted.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: She knows what happened, and your part of it is still on the record.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It goes down as a search two people agreed to, and you were one of them.

scenario.note: Do not argue with a parent in front of staff. Say your part and let the call end.

questions.q: A staff member says that if you had nothing to hide you would let her look. What is wrong with that?

options.text: Whether you agree is not evidence. The reason has to come first.
She is right. Refusing looks guilty and that is the end of it.
options.explanation: How something looks is not proof. Plenty of people say no for reasons that have nothing to do with guilt.

options.text: A refusal can be used later as proof that you did something.
options.explanation: Saying no is not evidence, then or later. What matters is what staff knew before they asked.

options.text: Saying nothing is the safer move, since it avoids the whole question.
options.explanation: Saying nothing does not avoid it. It settles it, in the direction you did not pick.

questions.hint: Which comes first, the answer or the thing that lets her ask?
questions.principle: Agreeing is not evidence, and refusing is not evidence either. Staff need a reason before a search, and whether you say yes has nothing to do with whether that reason existed. This matters because the line is persuasive. It can make saying no feel like an admission, and it lands hardest on people who have done nothing. Saying no politely admits nothing. You can say that in one sentence and leave it alone.

keyPhrase.quote: Saying no isn't evidence of anything.
keyPhrase.gloss: The reason has to exist before the question.

scenario.setup: The classroom doorway. Other students are walking past.

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: If there's nothing in there, you won't mind.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Saying no isn't evidence of anything.

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: So what's the problem?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: No problem. My answer is still no.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You said the thing that is actually true, in front of people, in one line.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You agreed because it felt like the only polite answer, and now nobody has to explain why.

scenario.note: This one is said calmly or not at all. It is a sentence, not an argument.

questions.q: A staff member tells another adult that you already agreed to the search. You did not. What can you do?

options.text: Say it again, out loud, in front of whoever is standing there.
Argue it out with her until she takes it back.
options.explanation: Arguing rarely changes what an adult writes down, and it can turn one problem into two.

options.text: Let it go, since saying nothing now keeps it simple.
options.explanation: It keeps it simple by leaving their version as the only version anyone has.

options.text: Wait, since a false report gets thrown out later anyway.
options.explanation: Nothing gets thrown out on its own. Somebody has to raise it, and they need something to point at.

questions.hint: Who else is close enough to hear it?
questions.principle: The version people remember is the one that got said in front of others. If someone says you agreed and you did not, the fix is short and immediate. Say it again, plainly, while there is somebody there to hear it. Not an argument and not a demand for a correction, just the sentence. Then tell a parent the same day, because a second person who heard about it that night is worth more than a perfect memory a month later.

keyPhrase.quote: I want to be clear. I did not agree to this.
keyPhrase.gloss: Say it in front of whoever is there.

scenario.setup: The gym hallway. Two adults are talking a few feet away.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: He said it was fine.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I want to be clear. I did not agree to this.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: You didn't stop me.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: That's true. I still didn't agree.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Two people heard the correction, which is what makes it exist at all.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The only version anybody heard is the one that is wrong.

scenario.note: Correct the fact, not the person. One sentence, then stop.

questions.q: A staff member says the conversation will stay between the two of you. How much can that promise cover?

options.text: Not much. She can be asked later what you told her.
Everything, because school talk never leaves the school.
options.explanation: A teacher can be asked by an administrator, by police, or in court, and has to answer.

options.text: All of it, because calling it off the record makes it so.
options.explanation: Naming it does not change it. What she can be asked about later is the same either way.

options.text: Whatever she does not write down stays between you.
options.explanation: Nothing has to be written down for someone to be asked about it and remember it.

questions.hint: Can she promise something that is not hers to promise?
questions.principle: Nobody at school can promise that a talk disappears. A staff member can be asked later what you said. It can be an administrator, the police, or a court, and she has to answer. That is not about her being dishonest. It is about what she can control, which is less than the promise sounds like. If this could turn into more than a school matter, talk to a parent and a lawyer. Those talks have protection this one does not.

keyPhrase.quote: Who else could be asked about this later?
keyPhrase.gloss: Nobody here can promise a talk goes away.

scenario.setup: An empty classroom after the bell. The door is half closed.

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: This stays between us.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Who else could be asked about this later?

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: Nobody, if you tell me now.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'd still rather wait for my mom.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Whatever happens next, you did not build it out of your own words.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The promise cannot be kept, and by then the words are already out.

scenario.note: You can believe she means it and still not answer. Both things fit.

questions.q: The school suspends you over what the search turned up. What does an unfair search do to that?

options.text: It can matter, but only if somebody raises it in the school process.
It cancels the suspension on its own, without anyone doing anything.
options.explanation: School discipline does not undo itself. In most places the court rule about bad searches does not reach it.

options.text: It does nothing, since only a police search can be called unfair.
options.explanation: A school search can be improper too. It is argued in a different place, with different rules.

options.text: It throws out everything they found, everywhere it might come up.
options.explanation: Nothing is thrown out automatically, and school discipline and a court case do not follow the same rules.

questions.hint: Who has to say something for it to count?
questions.principle: School discipline and a court case run on different rules. In court, a lawyer can argue that an improper search means the evidence should not be used. School discipline does not work that way on its own, and in most places that rule does not reach it at all. What can happen is that somebody raises it: a parent at a meeting, a written appeal, an advocate. That only happens if someone says it, in writing, on time. Ask for the decision and the reason for it in writing.

keyPhrase.quote: I want the decision and the reason in writing.
keyPhrase.gloss: If nobody says it, nothing happens.

scenario.setup: The school office. A suspension letter is on the counter.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Three days, starting tomorrow.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can I get the reason in writing?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It will be in the letter.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Okay. My mom is going to want to ask about the search.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: There is a letter to point at, and somebody at home who can point at it.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The days pass and the search never comes up anywhere.

scenario.note: Ask for paper. It is the one request nobody can talk you out of.

questions.q: A school search is starting and you have about five seconds. What is the order that protects you best?

options.text: Ask what they are looking for, say you do not agree, then let it happen.
Refuse to hand anything over until they explain themselves.
options.explanation: That rarely stops a search. It adds a second problem on top of the first one.

options.text: Say nothing, then explain everything once they are finished.
options.explanation: Saying nothing reads as agreeing. Explaining later adds your words to what they found.

options.text: Agree to it, then tell a parent it was unfair afterward.
options.explanation: Once you agree, nobody has to explain their reason. There is less left to raise.

questions.hint: Three things in order, and only one of them is about your hands.
questions.principle: The whole chapter fits in three moves. Ask what they are looking for, because the answer sets how far they can go. Say you do not agree, once, out loud, so nobody can say later that you offered. Then let it happen, because your hands are the part that can turn a school problem into a much bigger one. Tell a parent the same day. You do not have to know which rule applies or whether the reason was good enough. Somebody else can argue that later, and only if you did these three things.

keyPhrase.quote: What are you looking for? I don't agree to this.
keyPhrase.gloss: Ask, object, allow. Then tell a parent.

scenario.setup: Anywhere at school. A hallway, a classroom, the front doors.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: I need to look in your bag.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: What are you looking for?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Just open it up.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I don't agree to this. I'm not going to stop you.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know the size of it, you objected, and you got through it.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You improvise, and afterward there is nothing to point at.

scenario.note: Three sentences and your hands stay still. That is the whole chapter.

questions.q: You want to know what staff can search before anything happens. Where does the answer come from?

options.text: The handbook for what they will do, and the law for what they can do.
The handbook, since whatever it says is what the school can do.
options.explanation: A handbook says what a district plans to do. It cannot hand the school more than the law already allows.

options.text: Nowhere. Nobody has to tell you any of it ahead of time.
options.explanation: Districts publish this. It is usually in the student handbook, and you can ask the office for a copy.

options.text: The law only. A district cannot write rules about searches.
options.explanation: Districts write their own rules all the time, about lockers, parking, and phones. Those rules matter.

questions.hint: Two different questions here, and they do not have the same answer.
questions.principle: There are two answers and you want both. The law sets what a school is allowed to do, and it is the same for every district. The handbook sets what your district says it will do, and that part is local. A handbook cannot give staff more than the law allows, but it can tell you things the law does not, like whether lockers are treated as school property or what happens to a phone that gets taken. Reading it once, before anything happens, is worth more than any argument later.

keyPhrase.quote: Can I get a copy of the search policy?
keyPhrase.gloss: The law sets the ceiling. The handbook says what they will do.

scenario.setup: Your kitchen table. The school website is open on a laptop.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Where does it say what they can go through?

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Try the handbook. There's a section on it.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: It says lockers are school property.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Then that's the part to ask the office about.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You know the local rule before it matters, which is the only time it is easy to find out.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You find out what your district's rule is on the day it is being used on you.

scenario.note: Ask for the policy in writing when nothing is happening. Nobody minds the question then.

questions.q: The parking form you signed says you agree to searches of your car. How far does that go?

options.text: It covers the lot and the school bar. It is not a signature on everything.
It covers everything, since a signature is a signature.
options.explanation: A form is a district rule, not a blank check. What it can do is limited by what the law already allows.

options.text: It covers nothing, because the lot is not really school property.
options.explanation: The lot is school property. Parking there is exactly where the form is meant to apply.

options.text: It covers your car and your phone, since the phone was in the car.
options.explanation: A phone is its own thing. Being in a searched car does not make what is on it fair game.

questions.hint: You signed something about a car. What was it about?
questions.principle: Many districts make signing a form part of getting a parking permit, and many of those forms mention searches. A form like that is a district rule. It can shape what staff do in the lot, and it cannot hand them more than the law allows anywhere else. It is about the car, in the lot, on the school bar. It is not a signature that follows you into your bag, your pockets, or your phone. It is worth reading the one you signed, because they are not all the same.

keyPhrase.quote: I signed something about the car, not about everything.
keyPhrase.gloss: A form has edges. Find out where they are.

scenario.setup: The student lot after school. Your keys are already out.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: You signed the form, so this is covered.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: The form was about the car.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: It is.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Then I'd like to keep my phone with me.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The search stays the size of the thing you actually signed.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: One signature at the start of the year turns into permission for whatever comes up.

scenario.note: Read the form before you sign it, and keep a photo of it on your phone.

questions.q: Staff are going through your friend's bag and she looks over at you. What can you actually do?

options.text: Stay where you are, pay attention, and write it down afterward.
Step in and tell them they are not allowed to do that.
options.explanation: Stepping in rarely stops it and it usually turns one student's problem into two students' problems.

options.text: Leave, since standing there makes it look like you are involved.
options.explanation: Watching is not being involved. A witness is the most useful thing your friend has right now.

options.text: Answer for her, since you already know what is in the bag.
options.explanation: Speaking for someone adds your account to their situation. It does not take anything away from it.

questions.hint: What will she need tomorrow that only you can give her?
questions.principle: A friend being searched is the one time you are useful without saying anything. Staying and paying attention makes you a witness, and a witness is something a student almost never has. Stepping in is the move that feels right and it rarely helps: it does not stop the search, and it can put you in it. Afterward, write down what you saw while it is exact, and tell her to tell a parent. If she is asked to explain something, the best thing you can say is nothing at all.

keyPhrase.quote: I saw the whole thing. I'll write it down.
keyPhrase.gloss: A witness is worth more than an argument.

scenario.setup: The main hallway. Two staff and your friend's bag on a bench.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: Are you seeing this?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'm right here. I'm not going anywhere.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Keep it moving, please.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I'll wait over there.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: She has somebody who saw it, which changes what can be said about it later.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It is her word on her own, and nobody else remembers the details.

scenario.note: Do not film, argue, or crowd in. Stand where you can see and stay quiet.

questions.q: Staff hand what they found to the officer who works with the school. What is true now?

options.text: School discipline keeps running on its own, at the same time.
The school side stops as soon as police have it.
options.explanation: They are two systems and they run at once. Neither one waits for the other to finish.

options.text: Nothing you said to staff can reach the police side.
options.explanation: Staff can be asked what you said, and a school report can go with the thing itself.

options.text: Whatever they found proves the search was fine to begin with.
options.explanation: How it turned out does not settle whether it was allowed. That was decided before it started.

questions.hint: How many places is this happening in now?
questions.principle: Once something is handed to police, there are two things running. The school can suspend you on its own rules and its own timeline. A case can start separately, on different rules, and take much longer. Neither waits for the other, and winning one does not end the other. That matters for what you say, because an explanation given to settle the school side can show up in the other one. This is the point to stop explaining and ask for a parent, even if the school part feels small.

keyPhrase.quote: Is this the school part or the other part?
keyPhrase.gloss: Two systems, running at the same time, on different clocks.

scenario.setup: The hallway by the front doors after school. The bag is closed again.

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: I've passed it along.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Is this the school part or the other part?

lines.label: STAFF
lines.text: Both, probably.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Then I'd rather wait for my mom.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You stopped at the moment the second system showed up.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You explain the school part, and the explanation goes wherever the thing goes.

scenario.note: One conversation can land in two places. Ask which one you are in.
